where: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: Vehicles powered by gasoline and diesel give off air pollutants and gases such as oxides of carbon, nitrogen and sulphur, hydrocarbons and soot.
These pollutants affect the quality of the air we breathe, our health, crop yields and even the global climate.

where: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶2

sentences.text: Hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen react in sunlight to form ground-level ozone, better known as smog.
Smog is a major health hazard responsible for respiratory ailments and other illnesses.
Oxides of sulphur and nitrogen combine with water vapour to form acid rain, which damages our lakes, forests and crops.

where: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶3

sentences.text: Global warming is the result of too much carbon dioxide and other gases trapping heat in our atmosphere.
Global warming could cause average temperatures to rise, causing droughts, crop failures, lower water levels and more frequent and severe storms.

where: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶4

sentences.text: A car gives off less carbon dioxide than a larger vehicle, such as an airplane, truck, bus or train, does.
However, because so many people own cars and drive them so often, cars are responsible for nearly half the carbon dioxide produced by all forms of transportation.
Vehicles that carry large numbers of passengers, such as buses, produce less carbon dioxide per passenger than cars.

where: Driving efficiently › Intro · ¶5

sentences.text: As a driver, you can help to protect the environment from the harmful effects of driving by following these suggestions.
Many of them can also save you money.
For further information visit the Fleetsmart website.

where: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 1

sentences.text: Plan ahead.
Combine several errands into one trip.

where: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 2

sentences.text: Avoid driving during rush hours.
Driving in off-peak times takes less time, uses less fuel and releases fewer emissions.

where: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 3

sentences.text: Pay attention to smog alerts.
It is especially important to follow these suggestions on days when smog is bad.

where: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 4

sentences.text: For short trips, consider walking or cycling.

where: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 5

sentences.text: For longer trips, public transit is an environmentally friendly alternative to driving alone.

where: Driving efficiently › Before you drive · item 6

sentences.text: Carpool whenever possible.
If you want to meet at a central location, there are free carpool lots in many parts of the province.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 1

sentences.text: Avoid starting your vehicle unnecessarily.
A large burst of pollutants is emitted when a cold engine is started.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 2

sentences.text: Turn off your vehicle if parked more than 10 seconds.
Even in cold weather, vehicle engines warm up within 30 seconds.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 3

sentences.text: Obey the speed limits.
Driving at high speed uses more fuel and increases your chances of a serious collision.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 4

sentences.text: On the freeway, use your vehicle’s overdrive gear and cruise control for better fuel efficiency.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 5

sentences.text: Remove unnecessary weight from your vehicle, such as heavy baggage, wet snow and winter sand or salt.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 6

sentences.text: Maintain your vehicle’s aerodynamics.
Remove roof racks and compartments when not in use.
At high speeds, use your vents instead of opening the windows.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 7

sentences.text: Use your vehicle’s air conditioning wisely.
Use your windows and vents in city and stop-and-go traffic.
At high speeds, using your air conditioning is usually more fuel efficient than opening your windows and reducing the vehicle’s aerodynamics.

where: Driving efficiently › While driving · item 8

sentences.text: Don't “top-off” the tank when refueling.
Spilled fuel releases harmful vapours.

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 1

sentences.text: Regular maintenance will keep your vehicle running at maximum efficien­cy, reducing the fuel you need to buy and the pollutants your vehicle emits.

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 2

sentences.text: Keep your vehicle’s engine well tuned.
Worn spark plugs, dragging brakes, low transmission fluid or a transmission not going into high gear can increase fuel consumption substantially.

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 3

sentences.text: Follow the recommended maintenance schedule in your vehicle owner’s manual to maximize fuel efficiency.

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 4

sentences.text: Have any fluid leaks checked by a specialist to avoid engine damage and harming the environment.

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 5

sentences.text: Keep your tires properly inflated to reduce your fuel bill, emissions and tire wear.

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · item 6

sentences.text: Have your vehicle’s alignment checked regularly to reduce uneven tire wear and fuel consumption.

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · ¶1

sentences.text: (For more information on driving efficiently, see the section on maintaining your vehicle ).

where: Driving efficiently › At the garage · ¶2

sentences.text: Drivers are reminded that many collisions occur when the driving environment is less than optimal.
Whether driving at night, during times of reduced visibility or when road conditions are wet and slippery, drivers are encouraged to use the appropriate safe-driving tips provided in this handbook.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 1

sentences.text: Don't drink and drive.
Don't drive when you're taking medication that will affect your driving.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 2

sentences.text: Always wear your seatbelt and make sure passengers are using the appropriate child car seat,booster seat or seatbelt.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 3

sentences.text: Obey the speed limits.
Slow down when road and weather conditions are poor.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 4

sentences.text: Don't take risks: don't cut people off in traffic, make sudden lane changes or run yellow lights.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 5

sentences.text: Don't drive when you're tired, upset or sick.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 6

sentences.text: If you're in doubt, let the other driver go first - yield the right-of-way.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 7

sentences.text: Keep at least a two-second space between your vehicle and the one ahead.
To check your distance: start counting when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed object, stop counting when your vehicle reaches the same spot.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 8

sentences.text: Cut the distractions: don't overcrowd the vehicle or play loud music.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 9

sentences.text: Always check your blind spot: look in your mirror and over your shoulder before you change lanes.

where: Driving efficiently › 10 ways you can help make Ontario’s roads the safest in North America · item 10

sentences.text: Check traffic in all directions, including any sidewalks and paths/trails, before entering an intersection.

where: Traffic Signs and Lights › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: Traffic laws include the traffic signs and lights, pedestrian signals and pavement markings that tell drivers and other road users what they must do in certain situations.
This chapter shows you what many of those signs, lights and markings look like and explains what they mean to drivers.

where: Signs › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: Traffic signs give you important information about the law, warn you about dangerous conditions and help you find your way.
Signs use different symbols, colours and shapes for easy identification.

where: Signs › Intro · ¶2

sentences.text: Here are some of the many signs you will see on Ontario roads:

where: Signs › Intro · ¶3

sentences.text: A stop sign is eight-sided and has a red background with white letters.
It means you must come to a complete stop.
Stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement.
If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk.
If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.
If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.
Wait until the way is clear before entering the intersection.

where: Signs › Intro · image
Signs › Intro · ¶4

sentences.text: A school zone sign is five-sided and has a fluorescent yellow/green background with black symbols.
It warns that you are coming to a school zone.
Slow down, drive with extra caution and watch for children.

where: Signs › Intro · image
Signs › Intro · ¶5

sentences.text: A yield sign is a triangle with a white background and a red border.
It means you must let traffic in the intersection or close to it go first.
Stop if necessary and go only when the way is clear.

where: Signs › Intro · image
Signs › Intro · ¶6

sentences.text: A railway crossing sign is X-shaped with a white background and red outline.
It warns that railway tracks cross the road.
Watch for this sign.
Slow down and look both ways for trains.
Be prepared to stop.

where: Signs › Intro · image

sentences.text: There are four other kinds of signs: regulatory, warning, temporary conditions and information and direction.

where: Signs › Regulatory signs · ¶1

sentences.text: These signs give a direction that must be obeyed.
They are usually rectangular or square with a white or black background and black, white or coloured letters.
A sign with a green circle means you may or must do the activity shown inside the ring.
A red circle with a line through it means the activity shown is not allowed.

Signs › Information and direction signs · ¶1

sentences.text: These signs tell you about distances and destinations.
They are usually rectangular with a green background and white letters.
Other signs with different colours guide you to facilities, services and attractions.

Signs › Information and direction signs › Here are some common information and direction signs: · ¶3

sentences.text: Various exit signs are used on freeways.
In urban areas, many exit ramps have more than one lane.
Overhead and ground-mounted signs help drivers choose the correct lane to exit or stay on the freeway.

sentences.text: Advance signs use arrows to show which lanes lead off the freeway.
Signs are also posted at the exit.

Signs › Information and direction signs › Here are some common information and direction signs: · ¶5

sentences.text: Sometimes one or more lanes may lead off the freeway.
The arrows matching the exit lanes are shown on the advance sign in a yellow box with the word ‘exit' under them.

Signs › Information and direction signs › Here are some common information and direction signs: · ¶6

sentences.text: Freeway interchanges or exits have numbers that correspond to the distance from the beginning of the freeway.
For example, interchange number 204 on Highway 401 is 204 kilometres from Windsor, where the freeway begins.
Distances can be calculated by subtracting one interchange number from another.

Signs › Other signs › Here are some other common signs: · ¶1

sentences.text: The “slow-moving vehicle” sign is an orange triangle with a red border.
It alerts other drivers that the vehicle ahead will be travelling at 40 km/h or less.
When on a road, farm tractors, farm implements/machinery, and vehicles not capable of sustaining speeds over 40 km/h must display the slow moving vehicle sign.
Watch for these slow moving vehicles and reduce your speed as necessary.

sentences.text: EDR signs are used during the unscheduled closure of a provincial highway when OPP detour all traffic off the highway.
The EDR markers are located along alternative routes and provide direction to motorists around the closure and back onto the highway.

Signs › Other signs › Long commercial vehicle (LCV) · ¶1

sentences.text: This placard indicates a long commercial vehicle, which is a double trailer and can be up to 40 metres in length.
It is important to be able to recognize an LCV on the highway, based on rear signage, and anticipate both the extended length and limited speed when preparing to pass one on the highway.

where: Traffic lights › Intro · ¶1

sentences.text: Traffic lights tell drivers and pedestrians what they must do at intersections and along roads.
They tell road users when to stop and go, when and how to turn and when to drive with extra caution.

where: Traffic lights › Green light · ¶1

sentences.text: A green light means you may turn left, go straight or turn right after yielding to vehicles and pedestrians already in the intersection.
When turning left or right you must yield the right-of-way to pedestrians crossing the intersection.

where: Traffic lights › Green light · image
Traffic lights › Yellow light · ¶1

sentences.text: A yellow - or amber - light means the red light is about to appear.
You must stop if you can do so safely; otherwise, go with caution.

where: Traffic lights › Yellow light · image
Traffic lights › Red light · ¶1

sentences.text: A red light means you must stop.
Bring your vehicle to a complete stop at the stop line if it is marked on the pavement.
If there is no stop line, stop at the crosswalk, marked or not.
If there is no crosswalk, stop at the edge of the sidewalk.
If there is no sidewalk, stop at the edge of the intersection.

where: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶2

sentences.text: Wait until the light changes to green and the intersection is clear before moving through it.

where: Traffic lights › Red light · ¶3

sentences.text: Unless a sign tells you not to, you may turn right on a red light only after coming to a complete stop and waiting until the way is clear.
You may also turn left on a red light if you are moving from a one-way road onto a one-way road, but you must come to a complete stop first and wait until the way is clear.

where: Traffic lights › Red light · image
Traffic lights › Lights and arrows to help turning vehicles · ¶1

sentences.text: Flashing green lights and green arrows direct drivers who are turning.

where: Traffic lights › Lights and arrows to help turning vehicles · image
Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · ¶1

sentences.text: When you face a flashing green light or a left-pointing green arrow and a green light, you may turn left, go straight ahead or turn right from the proper lane.
This is called an advanced green light because oncoming traffic still faces a red light.

where: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · ¶2

sentences.text: Pedestrians must not cross on a flashing green light unless a pedestrian signal tells them to.

where: Traffic lights › Advance green light or arrow · image
figure: a green light with green arrow

where: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶1

sentences.text: When a left-turn green arrow is shown with a red light, you may turn left from the left-turn lane.
Vehicles turning left from the opposite direction may also be making left turns because they too face a left-turn green arrow.

where: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · image
figure: a red light with a left-turn green arrow

where: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶2

sentences.text: After the left-turn green arrow, a yellow arrow may appear.
This means the green light is about to appear for traffic in one or both directions.
Do not start your left turn.
Stop if you can do so safely; otherwise, complete your turn with caution.

where: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · image
figure: a red light with a yellow arrow

where: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶3

sentences.text: You can still turn left when the light is green, but only when the way is clear of traffic and pedestrians.
If the light turns red when you are in the intersection, complete your turn when it is safe.

where: Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · image
Traffic lights › Simultaneous left turn · ¶4

sentences.text: Pedestrians must not cross on a left-turn green arrow unless a pedestrian signal tells them to.

where: Traffic lights › Transit priority signals · ¶1

sentences.text: Traffic and pedestrians must yield to public transit vehicles at a transit priority signal.
The round signal is on top of a regular traffic signal and shows a white vertical bar on a dark background.
This allows transit vehicles to go through, turn right or left, while all conflicting traffic faces a red light.

where: Traffic lights › Transit priority signals · image
figure: a red light with a transit priority signal

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶1

sentences.text: Some intersections have separate traffic lights for left-turning traffic and for traffic going through the intersection or turning right.

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶2

sentences.text: When a left-turn green arrow appears for traffic in the left-turn lane, traffic going straight ahead or turning right will usually see a red light.
You may turn left from the left-turn lane when you face a green arrow.
Vehicles from the opposite direction may also be turning left.

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · image
figure: a fully-protected left turn light with green arrow

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶3

sentences.text: After the left-turn green arrow, a yellow light appears for left-turning vehicles only.

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · image
figure: a fully-protected left turn light with yellow light

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶4

sentences.text: After the yellow light, a red light appears for left-turning vehicles only.
Traffic going straight ahead or turning right will face a green light or green arrows pointing straight ahead and to the right.

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · image
figure: a fully-protected left turn light with red light

where: Traffic lights › Fully protected left turn · ¶5

sentences.text: In these intersections, you may not begin turning left after the green light appears for traffic going straight ahead or turning right.
If the light turns yellow while you are in the intersection, complete your turn with caution.

where: Traffic lights › Flashing red light · ¶1

sentences.text: You must come to a complete stop at a flashing red light.
Move through the intersection only when it is safe.

where: Traffic lights › Flashing red light · image
Traffic lights › Flashing yellow light · ¶1

sentences.text: A flashing yellow light means you should drive with caution when approaching and moving through the intersection.

where: Traffic lights › Flashing yellow light · image
Traffic lights › Blank traffic lights · ¶1

sentences.text: During an electrical power loss, traffic lights at intersections will not work.
Yield the right-of-way to vehicles in the intersection and to vehicles entering the intersection from your right.
Go cautiously and use the intersection the same way you would use an intersection with all-way stop signs.

where: Traffic lights › Blank traffic lights · image
figure: a blank traffic light due to power failure

where: Traffic lights › Traffic beacons · ¶1

sentences.text: A traffic beacon is a single flashing light hung over an intersection or placed over signs or on obstacles in the road.

where: Traffic lights › Traffic beacons › Flashing red beacon · ¶1

sentences.text: A flashing red beacon above an intersection or stop sign means you must come to a complete stop.
Move through the intersection only when it is safe to do so.

where: Traffic lights › Traffic beacons › Flashing red beacon · image
Traffic lights › Traffic beacons › Flashing yellow beacon · ¶1

sentences.text: A flashing yellow beacon above an intersection, above a warning sign or on an obstruction in the road, warns you to drive with caution.
